title: A Virus Makes Caterpillars Climb to the Treetops, Then Melts Them

scenes.text: These caterpillars climb to the treetops in daylight to die.
It makes no sense. Healthy ones hide in bark and soil all day so birds can't find them, and climb to feed only at night.
Infected ones go up and stay up. At the very top, the body liquefies and drips onto the leaves below.
It's a virus, and that drip is millions of copies of it, landing on the next caterpillar's dinner.
In 2011, scientists found the switch: a single viral gene. Take it out, and sick caterpillars die at the bottom instead.
Foresters have called it treetop disease for a century. It took one gene to explain the climb.

description:
Spongy moth caterpillars normally hide in bark crevices or soil by day and climb to feed at night. Infected with a baculovirus, they climb to the top of the tree in daylight, die there and liquefy, raining virus onto the leaves below.
In 2011 a team led by Kelli Hoover at Penn State showed in Science that a single viral gene, egt, drives the climb: caterpillars infected with virus lacking it died low down.
Which mind-controlling parasite should we cover next?
subject: moth caterpillar
